task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of November 12, 2024. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: The Clearwater Basin Aquifer, which underlies the Sutter Flats region spanning three states, has declined 14 meters since 2000 in the most heavily irrigated zones.
Helen Kowalski, 61, has farmed 1,400 acres in Sutter County for 34 years; she converted 600 acres to dryland wheat three years ago after her well began failing.
Kowalski said: "I didn't convert because of an incentive program. I converted because I had a pump pulling air. You adapt or you sell."
Neighboring irrigated wheat farmer Al Reyes, 47, is still pumping, but says his lift costs have doubled in five years as the water table drops and his pump runs longer for the same volume.

Reyes said he plans to transition to dryland farming within three years but does not know how to finance the transition: "The bank understands an irrigated wheat farm. A dryland farm in this county is unproven."

Sutter County water manager Dr. Patrick Brennan said the Clearwater Basin's decline rate suggests economically viable irrigation in the county's deepest-pumped zones will end within 15 to 25 years, and that voluntary conservation has not been sufficient to change the trajectory.
The county offers a well-retirement buyout program at $18,000 per irrigated acre; uptake has been slow, with 2,400 acres retired of a target 40,000.
Dryland wheat yields in the region average 28 bushels per acre — compared to 55 bushels per acre under irrigation — but production costs are also substantially lower.

Kowalski said her dryland operation is now profitable in most years, but that she had to restructure $340,000 in debt during the transition because her revenue dropped sharply before costs were adjusted.

Brennan said the county's most urgent need is a regional water monitoring data system that would give individual farmers real-time information about localized water table conditions, rather than relying on annual state surveys.

A University of Sutter extension agent, Dr. Lena Park, said dryland farming in the region requires a different crop calendar and different varieties; seed company catalogs for the region have historically offered fewer dryland options because the market was small.

Reyes said he has attended two county workshops on dryland transition but left both with the same question unanswered: what do I plant on 1,200 acres in a county with no established dryland processing infrastructure?
Two local grain elevators have told Reyes they are not equipped to handle certain dryland specialty crops; the nearest market is 90 miles away.
Kowalski said she is now seen by younger farmers as an example, which she finds both gratifying and uncomfortable: "I didn't plan to be a pioneer. I was just broke and out of water."

State agricultural officials say they are studying the buyout program's design; early data suggests farmers with smaller operations take the buyout at higher rates than large operators, because the fixed per-acre amount means less to a 3,000-acre farm.
Brennan said the county is already seeing groundwater quality changes in some areas as the water table drops, concentrating naturally occurring minerals including arsenic in remaining water.

Some economists argue that the transition to dryland farming would be faster if water rights were tradeable at market prices, creating a signal that reflected actual scarcity; current state law allocates water by seniority rather than price.
The USDA has offered transition assistance of up to $40,000 per farm through a pilot conservation program; Kowalski received this assistance and said it covered about 12% of her transition costs.
Reyes said he has not applied for federal assistance because the program requires a three-year farm plan and he does not yet know what crops are viable on his land under dryland conditions.

Brennan said the county is modeling what its food and tax base look like in 20 years if irrigation continues to decline; he said the projections are uncomfortable for local officials who depend on agricultural property tax revenues.
